newsitem.title: USA: Profit-taking pushes U.S. Treasuries down again.
newsitem.headline: Profit-taking pushes U.S. Treasuries down again.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower for the fourth straight day on Thursday, as players continued to book profits from the market's recent rally.
Bonds closed at session lows as attempts to rally late in the day failed.
The 30-year bond ended at 98, down 17/32 from Wednesday. Its yield climbed to 6.78 percent from 6.74 percent, its highest level since closing at 6.83 percent on June 11.
"The market is trying to get to levels where it can find customer interest," said a head trader at a primary dealer.
Treasury prices were lower from the start, as the market was somewhat spooked by a 14,000 decline in jobless claims for the week ended June 21 to 332,000.

Along with strong consumer confidence and home sales data earlier this week, some traders said the market has scrapped the notion that the economy will continue to slow, which would leave the Federal Reserve on hold for the time being.
"The numbers (lately) have been perky," said Bernie Jensen, head trader at Fuji Securities. "They are a reminder that the economy is not dead."
Jensen said it was a good bet the market would continue to consolidate over the next few sessions and "possibly shed five more basis points at the long end."
Yields at the long end have risen about 12 basis points, while short-term yields are up just five basis points, resulting in a widening of the two- to 30-year yield spread.
Traders said the short end was being supported by quarter-end buying, while large accounts liquidated intermediate- and long-term Treasuries.
"Whatever money is coming in is going to the short end," said a head trader at a large dealer.
Yet, he said, "The market has shown resilence on the way down; it has not gapped down. It has not been a bloodbath, just an erosion."
Traders said the market needed a correction, since it had reached levels regarded as not too expensive for the current economic envirnoment.
"The market had a good run up. People were getting spooked by the data so people took some profits," said a senior trader at a U.S. bank.
After the market's initial fall, Treasuries drifted through mid-afternoon when sell orders were hit as the September bond contract dipped to 111-9/32.
Helping bonds fall was hedging against numerous corporate and global bond issuance, market participants said.
Some players tried to buy on the dips late in the session, but lack of follow-through buying pushed Treasuries back to its lows of the week.
Activity was described as choppy amid average volume. According to GovPX, volume was about $83 billion at 1600 EDT/2000 GMT.
Trading on Friday was expected to be technical in nature again, as the market looked ahead to next week's June employment report as the next big event.
Data due on Friday include the University of Michigan's final June consumer sentiment index and the final reading on first-quarter gross domestic product, which is seen at a 5.9 percent growth rate.

In late trading, the two-year note was at 99-29/32, down 1/32, to yield 6.05 percent -- its highest level in three weeks. The 10-year note was down 10/32 at 100-31/32 to yield 6.49 percent. Bill rates were down two to up two basis points.
The new five-year note's yield was at 6.36 percent, up from 6.32 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
